title: my future self had already jumped
content:
anatomy of a bungee jump — fear as a portal to the sublime

by the time I actually jumped, I had already done it a thousand times, in my mind.

but let me back up, and tell you the full story. I have (or had) a fear of heights. bungee jumping off a 216m high bridge was not part of the plan, at all. while traveling together along the Garden Route in South Africa, my partner K (who has no fear of heights) really wanted to do this. our original plan was that he would jump — and I’d watch him from a safe distance and try not to feel nauseous.

this did not happen.

in the end, I jumped, and it felt like an initiation into the next phase of my life. it was cosmic, spiritual, sublime.

here’s how it happened, step by step.

“there’s no way I’m doing that”

the idea of bungee jumping came in the form of my friend Kayee (whose wedding we attended in SA, hi!!) suggested that we go bungee jumping at Bloukrans Bridge while traveling along the garden route. my partner K said “hell yes” while my auto-response was “no fucking way.”

for a week or so, I had the idea as an itinerary item for K, in my mind. I looked at google reviews of the bungee jumping site, and felt my heart beat accelerate, my and legs turn to jelly. K very lightly tried to convince me to do it with him, and then quickly backed off when I said no, but I’ll think about it.

instead, I looked up all the other things I wanted to do — zip-lining, hiking, kayaking, game drives, visiting this or that natural landmark. trying to plan a very busy few days was its own form of procrastination/distraction from my own fear. meanwhile, the idea of bungee jumping pulled at me, like a black hole.

a premonition of jumping

of course, I couldn’t stop thinking about it. over the next few days, as we filled our days with those other activities — a part of my brain was turning over this idea, again and again.

I’ve always had this visceral, pit in my stomach sensation whenever looking over the edge of a high place — a skyscraper, a mountain cliff — but at the same time, I’ve felt the unexplainable urge to jump. but could I actually, physically do this? do I really want to do this? is it not totally insane???

then, I went to a snake sanctuary. I had a premonition while holding a snake, and something happened. that moment felt like a poison cure for my fear — as in, I was afraid of the snake. then, in the moment I touched it, the fear instantly dissolved. I only felt peace, and a spiritual sense of pleasure.

after that day, I kept seeing myself, in my mind’s eye, jumping off the bridge. I had not decided to do it — my conscious mind wasn’t there yet. but my imagination was already throwing me off the edge; a deeper part of me had already decided.

my future self had already jumped.

by the time I actually did jump, I had already imagined it — a thousand times in my mind — diving into this place:

the reason why I decided to jump

in those next days, I felt a lingering sense that I had to do it, precisely because I was scared. more than identifying with my fears, I’ve always identified myself as someone who conquers and transforms my fears — as raw material, into my power.

I can’t count how many times I’ve talked about “leaping off the edge, into the unknown,” how much I use that metaphor of jumping in my creative work and life. I run a seasonal community, Labyrinth, about the unknown. I named my advising program Liminal Leap. I talk constantly about sharing your work into the creative void.

for this pathless path, the work IS, exactly, doing what terrifies you. I’ve been doing that my entire career. I would feel like a hypocrite if I kept using this metaphor — and when the actual opportunity came to literally jump off a bridge, into the unknown, I refused, because I was scared.

it’s not a question of “what would I tell my audience?” obviously, you wouldn’t know. it’s a question of, “can I live with myself???” — and “would I feel like a coward if I don't do this? is this symbolically significant to me?”

yes, I would. yes, it was symbolically significant. this was Scorpio season, and I’m a Scorpio stellium undergoing another year of transformative rebirth — as my uncertain visa status in Turkey means my next year felt like jumping into the unknown. if there was any time to jump, it was now.

edging towards the edge

we drove over Bloukrans Bridge at least twice before we actually went to the bungee jumping site. each time, I felt a full bodied anxiety. my body was saying no way, no way, no way. then, a few days after the snake sanctuary, we decided to drive there, to the bungee site, just “see it.” there was no pressure to jump, but I wanted to look. even that was an act of edging towards — rehearsing — the jump.

I stood there, looking across the bridge, watched other jumpers, asked a few nervous questions to the registration person. then, after half an hour, we signed up for the next morning — an 11AM jump. I could not believe it.

anxiety on the morning of the jump

I woke up at 7am, with full anxiety. I got my period the day before, and felt exhausted. I considered cancelling. K was very gentle with me, hugged me and said ok love, of course we can cancel. and I said, no, we’re doing it.

we had a slow breakfast at a farm. at the bungy site, they put us through a very systematic, organized process —

  • checking in

  • payment

  • getting weighed

  • having our weights + jumper numbers written on our hands

  • gearing up

  • waiting around with other nervous jumpers

  • a safety briefing at the edge of the bridge + taking a group video

  • walking across the bridge skywalk (which was its own ritual-like meditation on fear)

  • waiting at the jump site, at the edge, with our group

as soon as our group arrived, the staff turned on dance music and started organizing our 8 person group into two groups of 4 jumpers. there were three couples, and two men who came alone. couples were divided into separate groups — the women in the first group, the men in the second. I thought about this ordering for a while and wondered if it was a deliberate rule of separating couples. I mean… we all die alone. I read somewhere that 2 out of 10 jumpers make it to this point and decide not to jump. doing a hard thing alone (in our group) required me to be a little more courageous. I talked to the other women and we encouraged each other.

of course, we were all nervous as fuck, and the staff was magical in the way they exuded both highly systematic professionalism and — positive energy in the entire process. I read about this in the Google reviews, and it was absolutely what I experienced. they danced (was it part of the job description?), pulled people up with gusto, and were totally relaxed — like it was a very normal thing to jump off a bridge.

panic before jumping

all of that felt like a ramp up to the moment. I was jumper #4. I watched the three before me jump/fall — both from behind, and on the video screen — and felt my heart drop each time. it was really helpful to talk to them afterwards and see the exhilaration in their faces, to congratulate them on doing a hard thing, and to get their encouragement. community — even if very brief — actually does matter a lot when you’re jumping, metaphorically or not.

of course, the hardest moment is, absolutely, is right before the jump. as they prepared my feet and helped me approach the edge, every part of my body was in pure anxiety and terror. this felt like an insane thing to do, and my body was letting me know that it was not ready to die; it didn’t want to do this. the edge suddenly become a very real and terrifying thing — not just a beautiful projected landscape of my imagination. suddenly, the trees and sky and atmosphere had depth, and I couldn’t believe that I was about to fall into that depth. I was panicking.

the staff was remarkably well organized in executing the jump. after the safety checks, after four hops to the edge, while my brain was freaking out, I had two seconds before they started counting down — FIVE FOUR THREE TWO ONE BUNGEE — and at BUNGEE, one of the men lightly pushed me from the back, while I let myself fall.

no, it was not a proper kangaroo jump. it was active in that I chose to do this — and it was passive in that — I just fell.

the feeling of falling: terror & cosmic beauty

the first 3-5 seconds were absolute, pure terror. the fall didn’t end. if slipping on the street feels like a slow motion experience, than imagine this — each 1 second of falling felt as though it was 10 seconds long. I screamed like crazy. my hands were tingling. my body was absolutely certain that it was going to die.

around second 7, something shifted. I didn’t actually recognize the recoil of the bungee, or what happened, exactly, to my body, but my body did understand that it was not going to end here. and it understood that panicking and fear wouldn’t change anything. I let go. there was nothing to do, except surrender.

in that moment, my awareness suddenly shifted — from how terrified I was — to how cosmically beautiful a place this was, and how otherworldly my perspective felt.

I felt like I was an astronaut, seeing the earth for the first time, but very up close and near, so close I felt I could almost touch it — at 360 degrees perspective. when you look at a landscape from the top of a mountain, it appears flat, with a barely noticable curvature of the horizon. but when you’re suspended upside down, like the hanged man, falling and recoiling from the bungee, you’re aware of nature as a 360 degree, orbital experience, of thousands of trees, river, sky, and the wind and atmosphere itself, meeting me, inside a single minute in time. it felt like death and rebirth. it felt like an embodied awareness of the expansiveness of the universe. and in many ways, this perspective felt more real — on a cosmic, spiritual perspective — than standing with two feet on the ground.

after the jump

I was there, suspended in air, for 20 seconds or so, before a cheerful member of the staff came down to get me, asked me where I was from, and they harnessed me up. afterwards, they laid me on the ground of the bridge, helped me get up, and I felt the gravity of arriving back on earth.

I watched K jump, we walked across the skybridge, returned our gear, watched our videos, and slowly drove away. we celebrated with lunch and a beer in a tiny hamlet village by the beach, and had a slow rest of the day. my body felt the adrenaline rush for several hours. I felt shaky, and absolutely exhilarated.

integrating this experience

even beyond the cosmic experience of moving from terror, to surrender, to exhilaration, to spiritual, sublime beauty — I knew that this process of going from “no way” to actually taking the jump — would transform me in a deep, embodied way, even as my conscious mind didn’t know exactly how it would unfold.

I’m still sensing into the signals in my day to day life. I see the 360 degree astronaut perspective of nature, in my mind, when I close my eyes. I can go there now, anytime. I think about hard things I want to do, and I feel a sense of clarity and embodied confidence — that yes, I can do it. anything.

today, the day that I’m publishing this post — is my birthday.

this was my birthday gift to myself, this year. it’s my tarot year of the Hanged Man, and I can say that I know now, what gifts are waiting for me, in the process of surrender and suspension. my power is not in my fearlessness, but always choosing to inhabit and alchemize my fear. my fear is a portal that will take me somewhere sublime.
